channel.title: KSL.com - Utah News
channel.description: Utah breaking news and local top stories from KSL.com

item.title: California company awarded $100M to develop critical mineral facility on Great Salt Lake shore
item.description: The U.S. Department of Energy announced Thursday that Waterleaf P1 HoldCo, a subsidiary of California-based Lilac Solutions, will receive a $100 million federal grant to build a commercial lithium extraction and refining facility on the Great Salt Lake's northeastern shore. The project is one of seven nationwide sharing a $500 million pool aimed at expanding domestic critical-mineral processing and battery manufacturing, and its first phase is meant to double current U.S. lithium output. Officials tied the award to Utah's broader "Mission Critical" push to reduce reliance on China, which dominates global processing of rare earths and other key materials; Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said Utah hosts roughly 80% of the nation's listed critical minerals. The facility is designed to return processed brine to the lake with no net water loss, and EPA Deputy Administrator David Fotouhi said his agency continues working with the state on water and contamination concerns tied to the shrinking lake.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Utah governor 'deeply troubled' by Flock camera concerns, orders privacy review
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox said during his monthly news conference Thursday that he is "deeply troubled" by findings from the group Utah Civic Compact showing that 10 license-plate-reading cameras owned by the Weber County Sheriff's Office had been searched more than 5 million times since early 2022, mostly by out-of-state law enforcement agencies. Cox ordered the Utah Privacy Governing Board and the Utah Privacy Commission to review rules around the cameras, commonly called Flock cameras after the company that makes many of them, to ensure local agencies aren't misusing them. He said existing state law should already provide adequate guardrails but he'd support new legislation if the review finds gaps; two prior bills to further regulate the cameras stalled in the Legislature in 2025 and 2026. The news conference was Cox's first since a wave of primary losses by Republican incumbents in June, and it came the same week a Deseret News/Hinckley Institute poll showed his approval rating falling to 41%, its first time underwater.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff and Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox becomes a grandfather
item.description: Utah Gov. Spencer Cox announced during his Thursday news conference that his first grandchild, Finneas Spencer Cox, was born Wednesday. Cox, 51 and the father of four, grew emotional describing the birth, saying his grandson "had a little hard time breathing when he came out" but is doing well. The governor acknowledged he was distracted during the briefing, thinking about the new baby, and paused to compose himself at points. He used the moment to reflect on demographic trends of Americans marrying and having children later or not at all, saying he hopes "everybody gets a chance to be a grandparent someday" and calling family the country's most important institution.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Saratoga Springs boy being hailed a hero after saving brother, now recovering from own injuries
item.description: Six-year-old Zion Silva of Lehi is being called a hero after pushing his 4-year-old brother, Leo, away from a second-story window that gave way during a family gathering Sunday, taking the fall himself onto a concrete path below. Their father, Carlos Silva, said Zion suffered a fractured skull, a separation between his neck and spine, and a broken clavicle, and was flown by Life Flight to Primary Children's Hospital; doctors were relieved to find the arteries near his eye socket were undamaged despite the skull fracture. Leo initially downplayed the accident to relatives but later revealed that Zion had shoved him out of the way as the screen gave out, a detail that left the family in tears. As of the report, Zion remained hospitalized, off sedation but still on pain and anti-seizure medication, and had missed the start of his first-grade dual-immersion class he'd been looking forward to.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Babylon Fire closure area reopened after burning for nearly 2 months
item.description: The U.S. Forest Service lifted its special closure order for the Manti-La Sal National Forest's Monticello Ranger District on Thursday after the Babylon Fire, which had burned more than 100,000 acres, reached full containment. Forest Service spokesperson Holly Shyrer said all lands in the area are open to the public again, though isolated smoke may still be visible and crews will keep working in the zone to prevent new fire starts. She cautioned visitors to check weather conditions and stay alert, noting that while roads have been cleared of fallen logs, standing dead trees remain unstable and could fall on people who get too close. The reopening comes as more than 500,000 acres have burned statewide during Utah's 2026 fire season, with several large wildfires, including the Dugway Fire in Weber Canyon, still active; Weber Fire District wildland fire chief Lucas Minton said Dugway poses little threat to the public but will keep producing visible smoke as crews burn out debris piles.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Taylorsville man accused of holding woman hostage for 3 days, faces 20 charges
item.description: A 26-year-old Taylorsville man was charged Aug. 7 in 3rd District Court with 19 felonies, including aggravated kidnapping, forcible sodomy, rape and aggravated assault, after prosecutors said he held a woman captive in his home for about three days in late July. Charging documents allege he held a knife to her throat repeatedly, cut her arm, strangled and suffocated her, and raped her, leaving her with more than 40 documented injuries when police performed a welfare check on July 31. The woman told investigators she escaped through an open garage door while the man slept and called 911 while pretending to talk to her father, prompting police to respond. KSL is not naming the defendant to protect the victim's identity; prosecutors noted he has a standing protective order tied to the same victim from prior domestic violence convictions and a separate pending domestic violence case involving another woman.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: $238M upgrade of 5600 South, I-15 interchange in Roy nearly done, other projects continue
item.description: The Utah Department of Transportation's $238 million overhaul of 5600 South and its I-15 interchange in Roy is essentially complete after about three years of work, widening the two-mile stretch between I-15 and 3500 West to two through-lanes each direction plus a center turn lane and reconfiguring the interchange for heavier traffic. UDOT acquired roughly 60 parcels, mostly single-family homes, along the road's south side to make room for the expansion. Roy City Manager Matt Andrews and UDOT spokesman Mitch Shaw tied the project to growth west of Roy in West Haven and Hooper, plus the expanding Northrop Grumman Roy Innovation Center, where Sentinel missile defense work now employs more than 5,000 people. UDOT marked the milestone with a public celebration Thursday at Roy Elementary School, even as other regional projects continue, including a new 1800 North interchange near Clinton and Sunset and the northward extension of the West Davis Corridor to serve fast-growing parts of Davis County.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Utah has 'major gaps' in regulating noise, temperature from new data centers, agency head says
item.description: Utah Department of Environmental Quality Commissioner Tim Davis told a legislative interim committee Wednesday that the state has "major gaps" in regulating the noise and heat generated by new data centers, and that he plans to study both issues with help from state universities. Davis said the controversial data center proposed in Box Elder County hasn't yet begun seeking air quality permits, and that Wasatch Front sites face a tougher path because the region is already out of compliance with federal ozone standards, pushing natural-gas-powered projects toward other parts of the state. He noted Utah currently has no regulatory authority over data center noise, comparing the issue to homes built next to landfills, and said officials still lack full clarity on plans for the O'Leary-backed Stratos Project after its team declined an invitation to meet with his agency. Rep. Doug Fiefia pressed Davis on accountability given that no single agency approves data center projects, and Davis acknowledged the state needs to coordinate better, though he said Wednesday's hearing likely won't produce immediate policy changes ahead of the January legislative session.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Proposed Sugar House business district receives pushback from businesses
item.description: A Sugar House Chamber of Commerce-led proposal to create a special assessment district spanning roughly 700 East to 1300 East and Ramona Avenue south to I-80 drew pushback from business owners at a Salt Lake City Council meeting, modeled on downtown's Downtown Alliance to fund events, signage, holiday lighting and safety ambassadors. Utah Restaurant Association president Melva Sine said many Sugar House restaurants are still recovering from years of road and utility construction that ended in 2025 and need hardship grants rather than new fees, while bike shop owner Jeff Goddard said the same construction drove away customers he doubts events would bring back. Chamber co-chairman James Roberts has said the district would fund efforts to boost foot traffic and "vibrancy" in the neighborhood, with signage and lighting assessments potentially starting as early as 2027. Councilwoman Sarah Young noted the protest hearing is just one step in a roughly 48-step formation process and that the ultimate decision rests with affected business owners, who need support from at least 60% of the district's business property value to move forward.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Sen. Curtis talks public transit expansion ahead of temple open house and Olympics
item.description: U.S. Sen. John Curtis, a former Provo mayor and regular transit rider, told leaders of the Wasatch Front Regional Council in Salt Lake City on Wednesday that Utah faces "a real urgency" to boost rail and bus frequency ahead of the Salt Lake Temple open house and the 2034 Winter Olympics. Curtis said running trains every 15 minutes instead of hourly would make transit far more usable for visitors and residents alike, and pointed to legislation he's helped advance, including a bill supporting transit-oriented development that he said addresses affordability by putting housing near jobs and transit. He also criticized how the Federal Transit Administration's Capital Investment Grants program awards funding mainly based on existing ridership, arguing that formula disadvantages fast-growing communities that have planned ahead but don't yet have the population to show ridership numbers. Companion legislation for what he called the PATH Act has been introduced in the House by Utah Reps. Burgess Owens and Mike Kennedy, and Curtis said he expects transit legislation to move "rather quickly," benefiting even Utahns who never ride transit since every rider is a car off the road.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker, Deseret News

item.title: Logan man swims length of Bear Lake, prepares to cross English Channel
item.description: Open water swimmer Brayden Jarrett swam the full 19.5-mile length of Bear Lake in just over 11 hours on a recent Saturday, an accomplishment expected to be ratified soon by the Marathon Swimming Federation. His father and fellow swimmer Gordon Gridley, a federation official, followed him by jet ski, offering food, water and encouragement through a rough patch when a thunderstorm kicked up waves roughly 5.5 hours into the swim. The milestone is a training step toward Jarrett's four-year goal of swimming the English Channel, a roughly 21-mile crossing at its narrowest point that he has booked for June 2027 given the multi-year wait for a scheduling slot; he plans to prepare further with a November swim around Alcatraz in 61-degree water. Jarrett, who trains at Utah State University's HPER pool and Hyrum Reservoir, said open-water swimming teaches him he's in control of his own circumstances and gives him a sense of purpose unlike anything else.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Teen dies after falling around 100 feet while hiking Devils Castle Trail
item.description: A 16-year-old boy died Wednesday after apparently falling more than 100 feet while hiking the Devil's Castle Trail near Alta, KSL reported. The trail is a popular but exposed scramble route above Albion Basin in Little Cottonwood Canyon. Details on the circumstances of the fall and the emergency response were still emerging Wednesday night, and further information on the teen's identity had not yet been released.
item.dc:creator: KSL.com

item.title: Could a 'Super El Niño' deliver a big winter for Utah? Forecasters and resorts weigh in
item.description: Utah ski resorts and forecasters are watching what could become one of the strongest El Niño events on record heading into the 2026-27 winter, with Park City Mountain Resort targeting a Nov. 20 opening. Forecaster Evan Thayer of OpenSnow and Ski Utah said there's a chance this could be the strongest El Niño in 500 years, but cautioned that Utah's mid-latitude location makes the storm pattern's effect on snowfall unpredictable, pointing to the historic 1982-83 season as a boom year and 2015-16 as a bust. Thayer said El Niño winters often start slow before strengthening in February and March, and warned that the warmer temperatures the pattern tends to bring could offset any gains in precipitation. Resort officials say they're focusing on snowmaking capacity to bridge the uncertainty regardless of how the season plays out.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Twin brothers identified in Kearns funeral shooting
item.description: Family friends identified the two people shot outside a funeral in Kearns on Monday as 18-year-old twin brothers Vilisoni "Soni" Angilau, who died, and Vita Angilau, who remains in critical condition; both had recently graduated high school and were visiting from Seattle for a cousin's funeral. Unified Police Assistant Chief Justin Hoyal said the shooting stemmed from a dispute between two families: one of the twins got into a fight with a 17-year-old, and the teen's father, 45-year-old Afuhia "Rocky" Manatau, handed his son a gun, resulting in both brothers being shot along with the teen himself, who was also wounded and remains in critical condition. Manatau, who has an extensive criminal history, is in custody; police say the two families are distantly related and no longer believe the shooting was gang-related. Hoyal said a funeral attendee had warned an officer of possible trouble shortly beforehand, prompting police to station patrol units nearby, though the shooting happened on a side of the lot they weren't watching. Some members of the Angilau family have publicly called for forgiveness rather than retaliation, and a GoFundMe for the family had raised more than $12,000 as of Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Cambodia's first Latter-day Saint temple opens to the public
item.description: The Phnom Penh Cambodia Temple, first announced in 2018, held a completion ceremony on Aug. 12 attended by Elder Gerrit W. Gong and Cambodian government officials, and opened for public tours this week ahead of an Aug. 30 dedication by Elder Patrick Kearon. More than 2,000 people toured the temple on the first day alone, many traveling hours by bus. Missionaries first reached Cambodia in 1994, and church membership there has since grown to roughly 18,000 across two stakes; members say the temple spares them the long trips abroad they previously needed for temple worship. For a country still marked by the Khmer Rouge era of the late 1970s, several Cambodian Latter-day Saints interviewed described the temple, which incorporates traditional Khmer design elements, as a symbol of healing and hope.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Teen hospitalized with serious injuries after Roy car, e-scooter crash
item.description: A 14-year-old riding an e-scooter was seriously injured Wednesday night in a collision with a car near 5600 South and 2700 West in Roy, police said. The crash, reported just after 8 p.m., prompted lane closures in the area. The driver stayed at the scene and cooperated with officers, and police do not suspect impairment. Authorities haven't released the teen's gender or details of the injuries, and the investigation is ongoing.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: 'The future of healthcare': University of Utah opens $215M medical school
item.description: The University of Utah opened its new $215 million Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine on Wednesday, an eight-story, 210,000-square-foot building that university leaders and Gov. Spencer Cox described as ushering in a new era for medical education. Dean Kristina Callis Duffin said the building consolidates previously scattered facilities and gives more than 500 students across 26 departments access to simulation and hands-on training space, including a dedicated advanced simulation and anatomy center. Cox highlighted the health system's economic footprint, citing about 70,000 jobs and $7.6 billion in 2024 GDP impact, and noted U. Health trains roughly two-thirds of Utah's physicians. Half the project's cost, $110 million, came from a joint gift by the George S. and Dolores Doré Eccles Foundation and the Nora Eccles Treadwell Foundation.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Riverdale man sentenced to up to 15 years imprisonment in sexual abuse case
item.description: A Riverdale man, Joseph Ngoc Khang Nguyen, 33, was sentenced Monday to one-to-15 years in prison on two second-degree felony counts of sexual abuse of a child, to run concurrently. Nguyen pleaded guilty in June under a deal that dismissed a third abuse count and an attempted-abuse charge, stemming from an incident involving a 10-year-old boy in 2022. Charging documents cited a text message in which Nguyen apologized to the boy, and said he admitted to inappropriate contact with the child on three occasions during visits to the boy's home.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Feds officially acknowledge Utah immigrant detention center plans have been abandoned
item.description: A joint court filing Wednesday from Salt Lake City, Salt Lake County and federal officials confirmed what had been suspected since June: the Department of Homeland Security has dropped plans to convert a Salt Lake City warehouse into an immigration detention facility and will instead turn the site over to the General Services Administration as surplus property. The filing came in a lawsuit the city and county brought in June arguing DHS skipped required procedures in designating the West 300 South site. DHS hadn't explicitly confirmed the reversal before now, though it had signaled a preference for using existing detention space; a local attorney representing opponents credited sustained political pressure, while the Utah Democratic Party called it a win for local leaders. The case isn't fully closed — both sides are asking the court to pause rather than dismiss the suit until final disposition of the property is confirmed, with a status report due within 60 days if that request is granted.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Running is really getting their kids somewhere
item.description: An Orem couple, Sasha and Sarah Pachev, have raised 11 children as competitive distance runners, a tradition Sasha carried over from his own running background in Ukraine and Russia. The kids largely grew up treating daily runs as a routine expectation rather than an option, and several have gone on to notable success — oldest son Ben started at BYU at 14 and later earned a PhD, while other siblings earned scholarships or started college early. The family is also known on the racing circuit for competing in Crocs rather than running shoes, a quirk that started when young daughter Jenny refused to swap out of hers and performed well anyway; the inexpensive footwear proved practical for a family needing over a dozen pairs of shoes, and Ben has even placed in the top four of a half-marathon wearing them.
item.dc:creator: Peter Rosen, KSL

item.title: Utah-based Bricks and Minifigs reaches settlement with family whose allegations went viral
item.description: Bricks and Minifigs has settled the original claim brought by the Mansell family, who alleged the Utah-based Lego reseller failed to honor a consignment agreement and lost a Star Wars Lego collection once valued at roughly $200,000 — a dispute that went viral after YouTuber Ben Schneider (Reckless Ben) publicized it. In a joint statement, the company apologized and said mediation revealed the loss stemmed largely from how the collection was handled by the prior operator of the Salem, Oregon franchise involved, though it didn't disclose settlement terms beyond saying the family was compensated. As part of the deal, the Mansells assigned their claims under the original contract to Bricks and Minifigs so the company can pursue the franchise's former owners. The broader saga isn't over: the company still faces litigation with Schneider, who separately faces criminal charges tied to his efforts to confront company leadership.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: UTA considers first base fare rate increase in over a decade
item.description: The Utah Transit Authority is proposing its first base fare hike since 2013, from $2.50 to $3 for buses, TRAX, streetcar and FrontRunner service, potentially starting in 2027 pending leadership approval. Spokesman Gavin Gustafson said the increase is meant to offset 13 years of rising operating costs, pointing to sharply higher gas and diesel prices as one example of broader inflationary pressure since the fare was last set. UTA isn't yet addressing day-pass or ski-bus pricing and is separately exploring "tap to pay" contactless payment options beyond its current FAREPAY card system to make riding easier for occasional riders and visitors. The agency is also collecting public feedback on a related S-Line streetcar service change tied to a new station opening next year.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Fire in Uintah brings reminders of 2017 blaze, as firefighters preserve homes
item.description: Firefighters kept the Dugway fire from reaching homes in Uintah, Weber County, early Wednesday after winds calmed enough for crews to stop its forward progress, though the blaze came close enough to unsettle residents who lived through a more destructive 2017 fire in the same area. Neighbors described flames approaching within roughly 100 yards of homes near the train tracks before firefighters pushed them back. By midafternoon Wednesday the fire was about half contained after burning 15 to 20 acres, according to a state Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands spokesperson; the cause remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Utah State Hospital needs 'significant' increase in beds, lawmakers told
item.description: Utah State Hospital administrators told a legislative interim committee Wednesday that the Provo facility, with 378 beds, needs a significant expansion in capacity over the next several years, driven partly by a rise in court-referred patients facing criminal charges that has kept the hospital consistently full. Assistant superintendent Jeremy Christensen said the beds have stayed at capacity aside from brief pandemic-era dips. Hospital superintendent Dallas Earnshaw urged lawmakers to fund a 30-to-60-bed unit soon to address needs expected over the next decade. Earnshaw also flagged below-market pay for staff like nurses and security officers, even as physicians and psychologists are compensated well, as a separate concern for lawmakers to consider.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Ogden Valley leaders OK 512.6% tax hike, but Utah Supreme Court still has to weigh in
item.description: The Ogden Valley City Council voted 3-2 Tuesday to adopt a 2026-2027 budget that includes a property tax increase of up to 512.6%, which would raise taxes on an average $1.22 million home from about $105 to roughly $640 a year and generate an extra $2.48 million for the young Weber County city — though the hike's legality is still before the Utah Supreme Court. The Utah State Tax Commission had blocked the increase over a missed deadline in the city's incorporation process, a decision a lower court upheld before the city appealed. Councilwoman Kay Hoogland said the city has a backup "skinny budget" relying instead on a new transportation utility fee if the court sides against the city, though that option would raise less money and could only fund road projects. City officials attribute the shortfall partly to overly optimistic sales-tax projections in the original incorporation feasibility study, an issue several other new or growing Utah cities are also grappling with this tax cycle.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Utah finds a new economic and ecological partner in Argentina
item.description: A Utah delegation — including Department of Natural Resources head Joel Ferry, two state representatives and the Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity's Jeff Moss — returned from a 10-day trade mission to Argentina describing new momentum on two fronts: shared research into shrinking saline lakes and potential critical-mineral partnerships. Delegates pointed to similarities between the Great Salt Lake and Argentina's Mar Chiquita Lake, both large, shrinking, similarly salty lakes that host the same migratory bird species, and said Argentine researchers were eager to collaborate with Utah State University and the University of Utah on lake science. On minerals, Ferry said Utah visited ore-rich Argentine provinces as part of the state's "Mission Critical" initiative to boost domestic mineral processing and reduce reliance on Chinese refining, which dominates global output of rare earths and other key materials. Utah officials hope to return to Argentina within a couple of months and eventually bring Gov. Spencer Cox on a future visit.
item.dc:creator: Eva Terry, Deseret News

item.title: Bats prompt concern ahead of back-to-school at Stansbury Park Elementary School
item.description: Stansbury Park Elementary has struggled with recurring bat activity for years, and parents say bats have again been spotted inside the school, including the cafeteria, as staff returned ahead of the new school year; some dead bats have also turned up in the ceiling. Tooele County School District officials say they share parents' frustration and have spent the summer working with bat-mitigation specialists, the county health department and the state Division of Wildlife Resources on fixes, including installing one-way "bat doors" on the roof and sealing entry points. A state wildlife biologist said the migratory bats are drawn to the building's cinder-block construction and a nearby golf course, and that mitigation efforts appear to be working, though a few keep returning to look for their old roost. Officials say no illnesses have been linked to the bats, and while Utah's bat population can carry rabies, infection rates are extremely low; students are still advised never to touch a bat and to contact health officials if exposure occurs.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: 2 Bears Ears guides share differing perspectives on preservation of the surrounding lands
item.description: Two Blanding-based tour guides who are friends, Josh Nielsen and a guide identified as Williams, offered contrasting views on how Bears Ears should be managed following its 2016 monument designation. Nielsen argued the designated area is too large and favors more local input and multiple uses of the public land, though he believes the sheer remoteness of areas like Dark Canyon Wilderness will protect them regardless of official status. Williams, speaking near an ancient Pueblo kiva site, argued for stronger protections, citing the cultural significance of scattered and often-uncovered archaeological sites and voicing concern that reduced monument protections could reopen the region to mining interests, including uranium. Both guides said they're weary of the land's protected status becoming a political football with every change in presidential administration, and each called for more collaborative decision-making going forward.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Lehi High School students begin final school year in Alpine School District
item.description: Lehi High School students returned to class Wednesday for what will be their last "first day" before Alpine School District splits into three separate districts next year. Several student council members interviewed described the usual rhythms of a new school year — new schedules, friendships and responsibilities — and encouraged classmates, especially newcomers, to get involved in sports, clubs or other activities as the best way to make friends. Council members also highlighted school-spirit traditions like football games as a highlight of the year. Students framed the year as bittersweet: an ordinary first day that also marks the close of a chapter in the school's longtime district structure.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: 4 charged in 'long-term investigation' into Utah street gang
item.description: Prosecutors filed charges against four men in 3rd District Court as part of a long-running Salt Lake County gang investigation led by the Metro Gang Unit alongside Unified and Sandy police. Lauriano Robert Herrera, described in charging documents as a gang "shot caller" already facing an attempted-murder charge, faces the most extensive list of new counts, including weapons, drug-distribution and money-laundering charges, based partly on evidence from a court-authorized wiretap that allegedly captured him discussing gun and drug transactions and a past shooting. Co-defendants Eddie Alexander Ovalle, Martino Elliottt Godoy and Vicente Castro face varying weapons and drug-related charges, with a fifth suspect not yet formally charged. Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill pointed to the case in renewing calls for lawmakers to invest proactively in addressing organized gang activity rather than responding only after crimes occur.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah Senate president threatens critics with defamation lawsuits
item.description: Utah Senate President Stuart Adams sent legal demand letters accusing State Auditor Tina Cannon, podcast hosts Uriah Kennedy and Ingrid Bettridge, and a critic identified as Finlayson of making defamatory statements about him following his June primary election loss, threatening lawsuits if they don't retract the claims. Adams disputes assertions that he controls a state board, hid information about a new office location, pressured junior senators over reelection support, influenced legislation to benefit a family member, or concealed details about a data-center project from the public. Cannon responded that she wouldn't be intimidated and said she welcomes the chance to depose Adams under oath if he sues; Finlayson and Bettridge similarly pushed back, framing the letters as an attempt to silence criticism rather than correct falsehoods.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Moab man dies in Nevada car crash
item.description: Michael McCormack, 72, of Moab died Monday afternoon after losing control of his truck on state Route 305 about 24 miles north of Austin, Nevada. According to Nevada State Police, McCormack drifted onto the shoulder, overcorrected across the center line into oncoming traffic, then fishtailed into a skid that sent the truck off the road, where it rolled onto its side. He was not wearing a seat belt and was pronounced dead at the scene; the state's Major Incident Reconstruction Team is investigating.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Residents voice concerns over self-powered data center proposal in Spanish Fork
item.description: A marathon, six-hour-plus Spanish Fork City Council meeting Tuesday night — packed with overflow crowds — ended with the council tabling proposed zoning rules for a data center project near the mouth of Spanish Fork Canyon after nearly two hours of public comment that ran almost unanimously against it. City planning director Dave Anderson said the proposed ordinance amendment had received more scrutiny than any other the city has handled, and council members said they want to get the "guardrails" right before advancing. Volition CEO Jeff Chavez defended the project, saying it would be self-powered by natural-gas fuel cells that don't draw from the electrical grid or strain local water supplies, would generate about $44 million in tax revenue, and would include a company-funded community fund for causes like addiction recovery and housing support; the property owner said Volition is a better option than alternative buyers eyeing the site, such as a truck-heavy distribution center. Despite those assurances, most residents who spoke remained opposed, and the council said it would regroup its own questions before revisiting the issue at a future meeting.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom and Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Documented gang member faces 26 felony drug and gun-related charges
item.description: Justus Xander Solis, 18, of West Valley City, was charged Wednesday in 3rd District Court with roughly two dozen felony counts, including several weapons violations, maintaining a drug-involved premises, and 21 counts tied to distributing marijuana and THC products, after a Salt Lake County Sheriff's Office investigation into an Instagram account linked to him. Search warrants served in January and March turned up multiple firearms and THC vape products at Solis' residence, and charging documents describe him as a documented street-gang member with an extensive juvenile record who prosecutors say continued offending while on probation. A second man, Fabian Anthony Kelly, 30, who lived with Solis, was also charged with multiple weapons counts and misdemeanor drug possession after similar items were found in his room.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL
